questions.q: Which of these fractions is a fractional unit (a unit fraction)?
A shopkeeper cuts a 1 kg block of jaggery into 7 pieces of equal weight. How much does each piece weigh?
questions.a: 1/7 kg

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 1/40 of a cake is smaller than 1/30 of the same cake.
Reason (R): When the same whole is shared equally among more people, each person gets a smaller share.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: One metre of cloth is cut into 5 equal pieces to make flags. (a) Write the length of each flag as a fraction of a metre and write the division fact. (b) Write the matching addition fact and multiplication fact.
questions.a: (a) Each flag is 1/5 m long; division fact: 1 ÷ 5 = 1/5. (b) Addition fact: 1 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5. Multiplication fact: 1 = 5 × 1/5.
s: (a) Writes 1/5 m and the division fact 1 ÷ 5 = 1/5
(b) Writes the addition fact 1 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 and the multiplication fact 1 = 5 × 1/5

questions.q: A sugarcane stick 1 metre long is cut into equal pieces. (a) If it is cut into 5 equal pieces, how long is each piece? (b) If an identical stick is cut into 8 equal pieces, how long is each piece? (c) Which piece is longer, and why?
questions.a: (a) 1/5 m. (b) 1/8 m. (c) The 1/5 m piece is longer: the same length cut into fewer equal pieces gives bigger pieces, so 1/5 > 1/8.
s: (c) Says the 1/5 m piece is longer because the same stick is cut into fewer equal pieces

questions.q: One identical cake is shared equally in each of two groups. Each child in Group X gets 1/12 of a cake. Group Y has 3 fewer children than Group X. What does each child in Group Y get?
questions.a: 1/9 of a cake

questions.q: Rekha packs 1 kg of rice into 4 equal packets, and another 1 kg of rice into 8 equal packets. She says: 'A packet of the second kind weighs exactly half as much as a packet of the first kind.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The first packets weigh 1/4 kg each and the second 1/8 kg each. Folding a quarter into two equal parts gives two eighths, so 2 × 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4: two small packets weigh as much as one big packet. So a 1/8 kg packet is half of a 1/4 kg packet.
s: Writes the two shares, 1/4 kg and 1/8 kg
Shows that two 1/8 kg packets make 1/4 kg (2 × 1/8 = 2/8 = 1/4)
Concludes that Rekha is right: 1/8 kg is half of 1/4 kg

questions.q: For a school prize day, each of three classes gets one 1 kg box of peda to share equally among its students. Class 6A has 30 students, 6B has 36 and 6C has 40. (a) Write the share of one student in each class as a fraction of a kilogram. (b) Arrange the three shares from the largest to the smallest. (c) Two students of 6A are absent, so the 6A box is shared only among those present. Write the new share and say whether it is larger or smaller than before. (d) Among how many students should one box be shared so that each gets exactly half of what a 6A student would get with all 30 present? (e) The 6C teacher wants each of her 40 students to get at least as much as a 6B student. Can this happen by sharing one box among all 40? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 6A: 1/30 kg, 6B: 1/36 kg, 6C: 1/40 kg. (b) 1/30 > 1/36 > 1/40, so 6A, then 6B, then 6C. (c) 28 students share the box, so each gets 1/28 kg, which is larger than 1/30 kg because fewer people share the same box. (d) 60 students, because 1/60 + 1/60 = 2/60 = 1/30, so 1/60 is half of 1/30. (e) No. 40 is more than 36, so a 6C share (1/40 kg) is smaller than a 6B share (1/36 kg).
s: (a) Writes the shares 1/30 kg, 1/36 kg and 1/40 kg
(b) Orders them 1/30 > 1/36 > 1/40 using 'more people, smaller share'
(c) Finds 1/28 kg for 28 students and says it is larger than 1/30 kg
(e) Says no, because 40 > 36 makes 1/40 kg smaller than 1/36 kg

questions.q: Which fraction is read as '5 times 1/9'?
A block of paneer is cut into 10 equal pieces and Asha uses 3 of the pieces in a curry. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: She used 3/10 of the block, and the fractional unit is 1/10.
o: She used 3/10 of the block, and the fractional unit is 1/10.
She used 3/10 of the block, and the fractional unit is 1/3.
She used 10/3 of the block, and the fractional unit is 1/10.
She used 7/10 of the block, and the fractional unit is 1/10.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the fraction 4/9.
I. The number 9 tells into how many equal parts the whole is divided.
II. The number 4 tells how many fractional units are taken.
III. 4/9 is the same as 9 times 1/4.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
Match each amount in Column I with the fraction in Column II.
Column I: 1. 4 times 1/5   2. 5 times 1/4   3. 3 times 1/3   4. 2 times 1/7
Column II: A. 5/4   B. 2/7   C. 4/5   D. 1 (one whole)
(a) Name the numerator and the denominator of the fraction 11/15. (b) Write 11/15 as 'so many times' a fractional unit.
questions.a: (a) The numerator is 11 and the denominator is 15. (b) 11/15 = 11 times 1/15.
s: (a) Names 11 as the numerator and 15 as the denominator

questions.q: Gopal folds a paper strip 1 unit long into 5 equal parts, so each part is 1/5 unit. (a) How can he get parts of length 1/10 from the same strip? (b) How many parts of length 1/10 make a length of 3/5?
questions.a: (a) He folds each fifth into two equal parts; the strip then has 10 equal parts, each 1/10 unit long. (b) Each 1/5 holds two parts of 1/10, so 3/5 holds 3 × 2 = 6 parts of 1/10 (3/5 = 6/10).
s: (a) Folds each 1/5 part into two equal parts to make 10 equal parts of 1/10
(b) Finds 6 parts, since each 1/5 holds two 1/10 parts (3/5 = 6/10)

questions.q: Manav says: 'The numerator of 5/12 is bigger than the numerator of 2/3, so the fractional units in 5/12 must be bigger than the fractional units in 2/3.' Is he right? Explain using fractional units, and then say which of 5/12 and 2/3 is larger.
questions.a: No. The size of the fractional unit is set by the denominator, not the numerator: 5/12 is made of units of 1/12 and 2/3 is made of units of 1/3. A whole cut into 12 equal parts gives smaller parts than a whole cut into 3, so 1/12 < 1/3 and Manav is wrong; the numerator only counts how many units are taken. Writing 2/3 in twelfths, 2/3 = 8/12, and 8/12 > 5/12, so 2/3 is larger.
s: States that the denominator sets the size of the unit: 5/12 uses 1/12 and 2/3 uses 1/3
Explains 1/12 < 1/3, so Manav is wrong (the numerator only counts the units)
Writes 2/3 = 8/12 and concludes 2/3 is larger than 5/12

questions.q: Seema has three paper strips, each 1 unit long. She folds strip P into 4 equal parts, strip Q into 8 equal parts and strip R into 3 equal parts. She colours 3 parts of P, 6 parts of Q and 2 parts of R. (a) Write each coloured length as 'so many times' a fractional unit and as a fraction. (b) Which strip has the smallest fractional unit? (c) Show that the coloured lengths of P and Q are equal. (d) How many more parts of R must she colour so that the whole of R is coloured, and what fraction is that?
questions.a: (a) P: 3 times 1/4 = 3/4; Q: 6 times 1/8 = 6/8; R: 2 times 1/3 = 2/3. (b) Q, because it is cut into the most equal parts, so 1/8 is smaller than 1/4 and 1/3. (c) Folding each quarter of P once more gives two eighths, so 1/4 = 2/8 and 3 times 1/4 = 6 times 1/8 = 6/8; the coloured lengths are equal. (d) One more part, that is 1/3, because 3 times 1/3 = 3/3 = 1 whole strip.
s: (b) Names strip Q, since 1/8 is the smallest unit
(c) Shows 1/4 = 2/8, so 3/4 = 6/8 and the lengths are equal

questions.q: On a number line, the distance from 0 to 1 is divided into 6 equal parts. Which fraction is shown by the 5th mark to the right of 0?
Which of these fractions is marked between 1 and 2 on the number line?
True or False: On a number line, the point for 3/3 is the same as the point for 1. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. 3/3 is 3 times 1/3, and three parts of 1/3 cover the whole length from 0 to 1, so 3/3 = 1.
s: Reason: three parts of 1/3 make the full unit from 0 to 1, so 3/3 = 1

questions.q:
Assertion (A): On a number line where the distance from 0 to 1 is divided into 7 equal parts, the mark for 4/7 is closer to 0 than to 1.
Reason (R): The mark for 4/7 is 4 parts away from 0 and 3 parts away from 1.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Lata wants to mark 2/9 on a number line. (a) Into how many equal parts should she divide the distance from 0 to 1? (b) How many of those parts should she count from 0 to reach 2/9?
questions.a: (a) 9 equal parts. (b) 2 parts.

questions.q: On a number line, the distance from 0 to 1 is divided into 12 equal parts. (a) At which mark from 0 does 1/3 lie? (b) At which mark from 0 does 3/4 lie? (c) The fraction 1/2 lies at the 6th mark. Which of 1/3 and 3/4 is nearer to 1/2?
questions.a: (a) 1/3 = 4/12, so the 4th mark. (b) 3/4 = 9/12, so the 9th mark. (c) 1/3 is 2 marks away from the 6th mark and 3/4 is 3 marks away, so 1/3 is nearer to 1/2.
s: (c) Finds the gaps 2 marks and 3 marks and names 1/3 as nearer

questions.q: Gauri says: '5/6 and 6/5 are both close to 1 on the number line, but 5/6 lies just to the left of 1 and 6/5 lies just to the right of 1.' Check her claim.
questions.a: She is right. 5/6 has a numerator smaller than its denominator, so it is less than 1; it is 1/6 short of 6/6 = 1. 6/5 has a numerator larger than its denominator, so it is more than 1; it is 1/5 beyond 5/5 = 1. Each is only one fractional unit away from 1, one on each side.
s: Shows 5/6 is less than 1, one part of 1/6 short of 6/6 = 1
Shows 6/5 is more than 1, one part of 1/5 beyond 5/5 = 1
Concludes that Gauri is right: both are close to 1, on opposite sides

questions.q:
A cook in a school kitchen uses a tall measuring jug that holds 2 litres. On its side, the height from 0 to 2 litres is marked with 8 equally spaced lines, and the 8th (top) line shows exactly 2 litres. The jug works like an upright number line. Today the dal needs 3/2 litres of water and the sambar needs 3/4 litre.
(a) How much water does each gap between two neighbouring lines stand for?
(b) What amount does the 7th line show, and between which two whole numbers of litres does it lie?
(c) Up to which line should the cook fill the jug for the sambar?
(d) The cook says she must fill up to the 3rd line for the dal because the numerator of 3/2 is 3. Is she right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 8 equal gaps in 2 litres means 4 equal gaps in each litre, so each gap is 1/4 litre. (b) 7 times 1/4 = 7/4 litres, which lies between 1 and 2 litres. (c) 3/4 litre is 3 gaps, so up to the 3rd line. (d) No. 3/2 = 6/4 (multiply the numerator and the denominator by 2), so she must fill up to the 6th line; the 3rd line shows only 3/4 litre.
s: (a) Finds each gap is 1/4 litre (4 gaps in each litre)

questions.q: In the mixed number 4 2/7, what is 2/7 called?
questions.a: The fractional part

questions.q: A plumber has a pipe that is 25/6 metres long. How is this length written as a mixed number?

Consider these statements.
I. 31/8 = 4 1/8.
II. 5 2/9 = 47/9.
III. Every fraction whose numerator is larger than its denominator is greater than 1.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: Write the mixed number 7 3/5 as a single fraction. Show how you get the numerator.
True or False: The mixed number 3 1/4 is equal to 12/4, because 3 wholes make 12 quarters. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. 3 wholes do make 12 quarters, but the extra 1/4 must be added too: 3 1/4 = 12/4 + 1/4 = 13/4.

questions.q: Look at the fraction 29/4. (a) Is it more or less than 1? Give a reason. (b) How many whole units does it contain? (c) Write it as a mixed number.
questions.a: (a) More than 1, because the numerator 29 is larger than the denominator 4. (b) 7 whole units, since 7 × 4 = 28 quarters and 29 − 28 = 1 quarter is left over. (c) 7 1/4.
s: (b) Finds 7 whole units (28 quarters, 1 left over)

questions.q: Show that 9/4 cannot be written as a mixed number whose whole part is 3. Then write the correct mixed number for 9/4.
questions.a: 3 whole units = 3 × 4 = 12 quarters, that is 12/4. 9/4 has only 9 quarters, fewer than 12, so 9/4 is less than 3 and its whole part cannot be 3. Since 9 = 2 × 4 + 1, 9/4 = 2 1/4.
s: Compares 9/4 < 12/4, so 9/4 is less than 3 and the whole part cannot be 3

questions.q:
A sports teacher writes the long-jump distances of five students as fractions or mixed numbers of a metre. Convert each one as asked.
(a) Asha: 15/4 m, as a mixed number
(b) Bilal: 10/3 m, as a mixed number
(c) Chitra: 17/5 m, as a mixed number
(d) Dinesh: 3 2/7 m, as a single fraction
(e) Esha: 3 5/6 m, as a single fraction

For the school fair, a Class 6 group bakes nankhatai biscuits. One tray holds exactly 6 biscuits, and a stall is given only full trays. On Friday the group baked 29 biscuits and placed them on trays, filling each tray before starting the next one. The fair has 5 stalls, and each stall must get one full tray.
(a) Write the 29 biscuits as a fraction of a tray.
(b) Write this fraction as a mixed number.
(c) How many trays are full, and how many biscuits are on the last tray?
(d) Can every stall get a full tray? If not, how many more biscuits must be baked? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Each biscuit is 1/6 of a tray, so 29 biscuits = 29/6 trays. (b) 29 = 4 × 6 + 5, so 29/6 = 4 5/6 trays. (c) 4 trays are full, and 5 biscuits are on the last tray. (d) No. 5 stalls need 5 full trays = 30/6, but there are only 29/6 trays (less than 5), so 1 more biscuit must be baked to fill the fifth tray.
s: (c) Finds 4 full trays and 5 biscuits on the last tray
(d) Says no, compares 29/6 with 5 = 30/6 and finds 1 more biscuit

questions.q: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/7?
What is 15/35 in lowest terms?

Assertion (A): The fractions 12/20 and 9/15 have the same simplest form.
Reason (R): In both 12/20 and 9/15, the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Find the missing numbers. (a) 3/4 = ___/20 (b) 3/4 = 18/___
s: (a) Finds 15 by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by 5
(b) Finds 24 by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by 6

questions.q: (a) What are equivalent fractions? (b) Write one fraction that is equivalent to 5/8.
questions.a: (a) Equivalent fractions are fractions that stand for the same share or the same length, though they are written with different fractional units. (b) For example, 10/16 (multiply the numerator and the denominator by 2); any fraction such as 15/24 or 20/32 is also correct.
s: (a) States that equivalent fractions stand for the same share or length
(b) Gives a correct equivalent fraction of 5/8, such as 10/16

questions.q: True or False: Dividing the numerator and the denominator of 42/56 by 14 gives 3/4, and 3/4 is 42/56 in lowest terms. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. 42 = 3 × 14 and 56 = 4 × 14, so 42/56 = 3/4, and 3 and 4 have no common factor other than 1, so 3/4 is in lowest terms.
s: Reason: 42 ÷ 14 = 3 and 56 ÷ 14 = 4, and 3 and 4 have no common factor other than 1

questions.q: In Hostel A, 12 litres of milk are shared equally among 30 children. In Hostel B, 10 litres of milk are shared equally among 25 children. (a) Write the share of one child in each hostel as a fraction of a litre. (b) Write each share in lowest terms. (c) Does a child in each hostel get the same amount of milk?
questions.a: (a) Hostel A: 12/30 litre; Hostel B: 10/25 litre. (b) 12/30 = 2/5 (divide both by 6); 10/25 = 2/5 (divide both by 5). (c) Yes, both shares are 2/5 litre, so 12/30 and 10/25 are equivalent fractions.
s: (a) Writes the shares 12/30 litre and 10/25 litre
(c) Concludes the shares are the same (equivalent fractions)

questions.q: Farida says: 'The fraction 19/57 is already in lowest terms, because 19 and 57 are both odd numbers.' Check her claim.
questions.a: She is wrong. Being odd does not decide it; what matters is whether the numerator and the denominator have a common factor other than 1. 57 = 3 × 19, so 19 is a common factor of 19 and 57. Dividing both by 19 gives 19/57 = 1/3, so 19/57 is not in lowest terms.
s: States that lowest terms depends on common factors, not on being odd
Reduces 19/57 to 1/3 and concludes Farida is wrong

questions.q: At a village festival, four groups of children share buttermilk equally. Group P shares 6 litres among 8 children, Group Q shares 9 litres among 12 children, Group R shares 10 litres among 14 children and Group S shares 15 litres among 20 children. (a) Write the share of one child in each group as a fraction of a litre. (b) Write each share in lowest terms. (c) In which groups does every child get the same amount? (d) Does a child in the remaining group get more or less than the others, and by how much? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) P: 6/8, Q: 9/12, R: 10/14, S: 15/20 litre. (b) 6/8 = 3/4, 9/12 = 3/4, 10/14 = 5/7, 15/20 = 3/4. (c) Groups P, Q and S: each child gets 3/4 litre. (d) Less. With the common denominator 28, 5/7 = 20/28 and 3/4 = 21/28; since 20/28 < 21/28, a child in Group R gets 1/28 litre less.
s: (c) Names P, Q and S as getting the same share, 3/4 litre
(d) Compares 20/28 with 21/28 and finds R gets 1/28 litre less

questions.q: Which is greater, 5/11 or 8/11, and why?
questions.a: 8/11, because both use the fractional unit 1/11 and 8 such units are more than 5
o: 8/11, because both use the fractional unit 1/11 and 8 such units are more than 5
5/11, because a smaller numerator means each fractional unit is bigger
They are equal, because the two fractions have the same denominator

questions.q: Which number can be used as a common denominator to compare 2/3 and 3/7?
Three friends are reading the same storybook. Arun has finished 4/9 of it, Bela 1/2 of it and Chand 5/12 of it. Which list goes from the one who has read the most to the one who has read the least?
questions.a: Bela, Arun, Chand

questions.q:
Match each pair of fractions in Column I with the same pair written with a common denominator in Column II.
Column I: 1. 3/5 and 2/3   2. 3/4 and 5/6   3. 1/2 and 4/9   4. 3/8 and 2/5
Column II: A. 9/18 and 8/18   B. 15/40 and 16/40   C. 9/15 and 10/15   D. 9/12 and 10/12
True or False: 9/13 is greater than 7/10, because 9 is greater than 7 and 13 is greater than 10. Give the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. With the common denominator 130, 9/13 = 90/130 and 7/10 = 91/130. Since 90 < 91, 9/13 is smaller than 7/10; comparing the numerators and the denominators separately does not work.

questions.q: (a) Write 2/5 and 3/8 with the common denominator 40. (b) Which of the two fractions is greater? (c) By how many fortieths is it greater?

In Group 1, 3 melons are shared equally among 4 children. In Group 2, 5 melons are shared equally among 4 children. (a) Write the share of one child in each group. (b) In which group does each child get more, and why?
questions.a: (a) Group 1: 3/4 of a melon; Group 2: 5/4 of a melon. (b) Group 2: the number of children is the same but more melons are shared, so each share is larger (5/4 > 3/4).
s: (a) Writes the shares 3/4 and 5/4 of a melon
(b) Names Group 2, because the same number of children share more melons

questions.q: Pallavi says: 'To compare 4/9 and 5/12, the only common denominator I can use is 9 × 12 = 108, and it shows that 4/9 is the greater fraction.' Which part of her claim is right and which part is wrong? Show your working.
questions.a: She is partly right. With 108: 4/9 = 48/108 and 5/12 = 45/108, so 4/9 is greater; that part is right. But 108 is not the only choice: 36 is also a common multiple of 9 and 12, and with 36, 4/9 = 16/36 and 5/12 = 15/36, which gives the same result. So 'the only common denominator' is wrong.
s: Shows 4/9 = 48/108 and 5/12 = 45/108, so 4/9 is greater (this part is right)
Names a smaller common denominator, 36, as a common multiple of 9 and 12
Shows 16/36 > 15/36 and concludes her claim is partly right: 'only 108' is wrong

questions.q: Four sections of Class 6 collect old newspapers for recycling, and every section has the same target. By Friday, 6A has reached 5/9 of its target, 6B 7/12, 6C 2/3 and 6D 11/18. (a) Find one common denominator for all four fractions and say why it works. (b) Write each fraction with that denominator. (c) Arrange the sections from the one closest to its target to the one farthest from it. (d) Which sections have collected more than 6B? (e) What more fraction of its target must 6A collect to catch up with the leading section? Give the answer in lowest terms.
s: (a) Chooses 36 and says 9, 12, 3 and 18 all divide it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 5/9 − 2/9 = 3/9, which is 1/3 in lowest terms.
Reason (R): When two fractions with the same denominator are subtracted, the denominator of the answer is the difference of the two denominators.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. 2/9 + 4/9 = 6/9, which is 2/3 in lowest terms.
II. 1/2 + 1/5 = 2/7.
III. 7/8 − 3/8 = 1/2.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: Add 3/8 and 1/4 using Brahmagupta's method.

Ira spends 5/6 hour on her maths homework and 2/5 hour on her science homework. (a) How much time does she spend on the two subjects together? Write it as a mixed number. (b) How much longer does she spend on maths than on science?
questions.a: (a) With the common denominator 30: 5/6 = 25/30 and 2/5 = 12/30, so the total is 37/30 = 1 7/30 hours. (b) 25/30 − 12/30 = 13/30 hour.

questions.q: (a) Find 5/12 + 4/12. (b) Find 9/10 − 2/10. (c) Write your answer to (a) in lowest terms.

An electrician has a 1-metre piece of wire. He cuts 3/10 m of it for a switch board and 1/4 m for a doorbell. He then needs 2/5 m for a fan. (a) How much wire has he used for the switch board and the doorbell together? (b) How much wire is left? (c) Is the wire left enough for the fan? (d) How much wire will remain after the fan piece is cut?

Meera can walk to school by two routes. Route A is 2/5 km along the main road and then 1/4 km through a lane. Route B is 1/2 km along the canal and then 1/6 km past the market. (a) Find the length of Route A. (b) Find the length of Route B in lowest terms. (c) Which route is shorter, and by how much? (d) If Meera takes Route A to school and back home, how far does she walk? Write it as a mixed number in lowest terms. (e) Her mother says: 'Take the canal route (Route B) if it is less than 1/10 km longer than Route A, because it has no traffic.' Which route should Meera take? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 2/5 + 1/4 = 8/20 + 5/20 = 13/20 km. (b) 1/2 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3 km. (c) With the denominator 60: 13/20 = 39/60 and 2/3 = 40/60, so Route A is shorter by 1/60 km. (d) 13/20 + 13/20 = 26/20 = 1 6/20 = 1 3/10 km. (e) Route B is longer by only 1/60 km, and 1/10 = 6/60, so 1/60 < 1/10; she should take Route B.
s: (c) Compares 39/60 with 40/60: Route A shorter by 1/60 km
(e) Compares 1/60 with 1/10 = 6/60 and decides on Route B

questions.q:
For a Diwali rangoli, Class 6 buys coloured powder in packets: red 3/8 kg, yellow 1/8 kg and white 2/8 kg. The finished rangoli design needs 1 kg of powder in all. The class decides that the red and yellow powders will be used for the border and the white powder for the centre.
(a) How much powder will be used for the border?
(b) How much powder has the class bought in all? Write it in lowest terms.
(c) How much more red powder is there than white powder?
(d) Is the powder bought enough for the design? If not, how much more is needed?
s: (a) Finds 4/8 kg (1/2 kg) for the border
(c) Finds 1/8 kg more red than white
(d) Says no and finds 2/8 = 1/4 kg more is needed
